questions.q: For an 814 mm2 GH100 die, an illustrative D0 = 0.1/cm2 model gives about 45% perfect-die yield. How can a model of sellable yield be higher when the product enables fewer SMs than physically exist?
options: TSMC's 4N process has a defect density an order of magnitude below the industry norm
The die is built with 144 SMs and 6 HBM controllers but ships with 132 SMs and 5 HBM stacks enabled, so dies with defects in the spare SMs or one memory partition are still sellable
NVIDIA uses a two-die design so that only one of the pair must be defect-free
Wafer sort rejects only dies with defects in the L2 cache, and all other defects are corrected in firmware
questions.explanation: Designed-in redundancy can allow suitable dies with localized defects to be sold with resources disabled. The 65–80% and 40–50 dies-per-wafer figures in the module are illustrative modeling results, not disclosed NVIDIA production yield. Defect location, clustering and non-redundant regions still matter.

questions.q: In the physical design flow, what does DRC/LVS signoff (typically in Siemens Calibre) verify that synthesis, place-and-route, and static timing analysis do not?
options: That every polygon obeys the foundry's geometric rules (widths, spacings, densities, multi-patterning constraints) and that the transistors and wires extracted from the layout match the gate-level netlist
That all setup and hold timing paths meet the clock period across process corners
That IR drop from the C4 bumps to the transistors stays within ~5-10% of Vdd
That the RTL is functionally equivalent to the C++ performance model
questions.explanation: DRC checks the geometry against the PDK rule deck; LVS proves the layout implements the netlist. Timing is PrimeTime/Tempus, IR drop is RedHawk/Voltus, and functional equivalence is checked by simulation, emulation, and formal tools.

questions.q: Why does Blackwell B200 require CoWoS-L rather than the CoWoS-S used for H100?
options: CoWoS-L supports HBM3E while CoWoS-S only supports HBM3

The two reticle-limited dies plus eight HBM stacks need ~3.3 reticles of interposer, at which a whole-silicon reticle-stitched interposer becomes too costly and low-yielding, so TSMC puts silicon only where fine wiring is needed: small silicon bridges (LSI) embedded in an organic RDL interposer under the die-to-die and HBM edges, carrying the 10 TB/s NV-HBI link
CoWoS-L is cheaper per package, which offsets the higher HBM cost
CoWoS-S cannot dissipate more than 700 W
questions.explanation: CoWoS-S interposers are already reticle-stitched (H100's is ~2.5 reticles of silicon); at ~3.3 reticles a whole-silicon slab's cost and defect-driven yield loss become prohibitive, and only the strips under the die-to-die and die-to-HBM edges need silicon-fine wiring. CoWoS-L therefore uses an organic RDL interposer with local silicon bridges only at those edges. It is more expensive per package than CoWoS-S, but it is the practical way to build a ~3.3-reticle package.

questions.q: The GB200 NVL72 uses roughly 5,000 passive copper cables (about 2 miles) for its NVLink spine instead of optical links. What is the primary engineering consequence of that choice?
options: The rack can be air-cooled because copper cables generate no heat
The NVLink domain must extend across many racks because copper has longer reach than fiber

Passive copper at 200 Gb/s per lane reaches only ~1-1.5 m, which confines the 72-GPU NVLink domain to one rack and drives the ~120-140 kW power density that forces direct liquid cooling, in exchange for saving ~20 kW of transceiver power and a large fraction of the cost
Copper limits NVLink bandwidth to 900 GB/s per GPU
questions.explanation: The reach limit of copper is the reason NVL72 is a single very dense rack. Avoiding thousands of ~15-20 W optical transceivers saves power and money, but concentrating 72 GPUs, 36 CPUs, and 18 switch chips in one enclosure makes cold plates and CDUs mandatory.

questions.q: Public BOM estimates put an H100 SXM at ~$3,000-3,500 to manufacture against a ~$25-30k price. Which statement about the cost structure is correct?
options: The GPU die is the largest cost because a 4N wafer costs ~$16-17k
The five HBM3 stacks (~$1,300-2,000) are the largest item, CoWoS plus substrate is ~$500-1,000, and the GPU die is only ~$300-400, about 10% of the total
Test and burn-in exceed the cost of the die and memory combined
The SXM board and VRM are roughly half of the total
questions.explanation: In this illustrative public cost breakdown, memory and packaging exceed the compute die cost. These estimates do not establish NVIDIA product-level COGS or gross margin, and a cost share does not by itself establish which factory resource limits output.

questions.q: An H100 SM runs at ~1.8 GHz, so the clock period is ~555 ps. Why do designers have only ~465 ps of that for logic on each path, and what is the escalating sequence of fixes when a path does not fit?
options: The clock is only 84% duty cycle; failing paths are fixed by raising the supply voltage in the VRM firmware

The flip-flop's clock-to-output delay (~40 ps), the next flip-flop's setup margin (~20 ps), and clock skew plus jitter (~30 ps) are subtracted first; a failing path is fixed by upsizing cells, inserting repeaters, re-placing cells closer together, and, as a last resort, changing the RTL, which restarts the emulation compile
Parasitic extraction adds a fixed 90 ps to every path; failing paths are fixed by adding another metal layer to the PDK
The emulator can only run at 465 ps per cycle; failing paths are fixed by moving them to a slower clock domain
questions.explanation: Only the time between one flip-flop's output becoming valid and the next flip-flop's setup deadline is available for gates and wires, and skew and jitter eat into it. At ~15-25 ps per 4N gate that is ~20-30 levels of logic per cycle, and a wire across a 1-2 mm SM can cost ~100 ps on its own, which is why blocks are kept small and why timing closure is the largest schedule risk in physical design.

questions.q: In 2023 the quoted lead time for an H100 reached ~52 weeks. What was that 52 weeks actually made of?
options: 52 weeks of wafer processing, because an 80-mask-layer N4 flow takes about a year

About 6 months of physical cycle time from wafer start to a GPU on a board, with the remainder being queueing for CoWoS packaging and HBM allocation and the ~12-month capacity commitments the chain requires
26 weeks in the fab and 26 weeks of burn-in and system-level test
Mostly the ~3-month tape-out-to-first-silicon delay repeated for each stepping
questions.explanation: Cycle time (how long a unit of material spends moving through the chain) is ~6 months to a GPU on a board and ~7+ to a burned-in rack. Lead time was longer because HBM wafers, substrates and CoWoS slots must be primed months ahead and NVIDIA commits to TSMC wafer and CoWoS capacity a year or more out; the queue was for allocation, not processing.

questions.q: A GB200 NVL72 rack draws ~130 kW and ~85% of that heat leaves through the liquid loop. Water carries 4.18 kJ per kg per degree C. If the coolant is allowed to warm by 10 degrees C between inlet and outlet, roughly what flow does one rack need?
options: ~16 L/min, about a kitchen tap
~160 L/min (about 2.6 kg/s), roughly a bathtub of water per minute
~1,600 L/min, which is why NVL72 needs a dedicated facility water main per rack
~2 L/min, since most of the heat is removed by the CDU's refrigeration cycle
questions.explanation: ~110 kW into the water divided by (4.18 kJ/kg-K x 10 K) gives ~2.6 kg/s, about 160 L/min per rack; 770 racks in a 100 MW site move ~2 m3/s. The CDU is a heat exchanger and pump set, not a refrigerator, and the flow arithmetic is what sizes the manifolds, pumps and pipes of a liquid-cooled data center.
